prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and the invention of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that made it a treatment for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep B028 as a single prize part and I keep it first on the merits. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through glucose-dependent insulin secretion and effects on appetite and gastric emptying, to drugs with randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is settled and the timing is right. Having read the whole first round, I still prefer Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. Holst and Drucker carry the physiology. Knudsen carries the step that made the physiology a medicine: turning a peptide with a half-life of minutes into an agent that works once a week required new insight into DPP-4 resistance and albumin binding, and that insight is why the discovery now matters to patients. This reading also avoids placing the committee in the middle of the Mojsov and Habener priority dispute, which the supplied text cannot settle. Because the three-name cap is already used, this is a one-part prize.
statement.case_against: Five of six colleagues now name Mojsov, and I take that seriously, although I do not treat the count as a scientific argument. The strongest objection to my trio is that Knudsen's contribution is development inside a company and that a citation including it can be read as rewarding commercial success. Habener is outside the credited names and every trio is open to the charge that the proglucagon and peptide work is under-credited. My configuration leaves the active-peptide identification, which is a discovery, without a named laureate, and a committee that wants a discovery-only prize has a better-fitting trio in Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I would accept that trio, and I cannot show from the supplied record that mine is the only defensible choice.

responses.point: You moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov so that the citation rewards discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form rather than a company's drug design.
responses.response: I understand the move and I have weighed it, since we started from the same trio. I do not think the choice is between discovery and a company's design. The long-acting agonists are the evidence that the physiology matters, and the conversion of the native peptide was an inventive step, not routine engineering. The Mojsov alternative also rests on a priority question that you and I both say we cannot resolve from the text, so it replaces one attribution risk with another. I stay with Knudsen, and if the committee follows your trio I would not oppose it.

responses.point: The committee should state clearly whether it is rewarding discovery or development, and a physiology-only trio leaves out the step that produced liraglutide and semaglutide.
responses.response: This is the question I think we should settle first, and your note that a three-person physiology prize omits the step behind the drugs supports my reading. My answer is that the citation should reward both, in a single sentence, because the achievement honoured is the physiology and its conversion into therapy, not either half alone. You prefer Mojsov in the third seat. The difference between us is therefore about the citation, not the science, and I think your own uncertainty about fair allocation argues for the version that does not depend on the disputed peptide priority.

responses.point: An industry scientist on the prize changes its character, and B045 with a June and Sadelain pairing has fewer credit problems than GLP-1.
responses.response: On the first point, I agree that it is a real consideration, but neither the rules nor precedent exclude it and the issue is the nature of the contribution. I judge Knudsen's contribution to be one of invention rather than only scale-up. On B045, I agree June and Sadelain is the cleaner pair, with Rosenberg's TIL work being a separate lineage and Eshhar uncredited. But the cap makes a two-part prize with B028 impossible, since B028 takes three names, and I do not think a cleaner second candidate is a reason to weaken the first. I would keep B045 as my first alternative for a later year.

responses.point: A prize on a drug class with a very large commercial footprint may be read as rewarding commercial success, and long-term safety and durability after discontinuation remain open.
responses.response: I share both concerns. The commercial point is why I want the citation to name the scientific step, the physiology and the invention of the long-acting agonist, and not the products. On durability, the outcome trials and the mechanism are settled enough for the prize while the long-term safety questions you raise are still being worked out. They apply to most therapies the prize has honoured at a comparable stage, and I do not see them as a reason to wait.

uncertainties: Fair allocation among Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen and the uncredited Habener cannot be resolved from the supplied text, and I have not verified the priority history independently.
Whether the committee prefers a discovery-only citation or one that includes development, which determines the third name.
Whether the committee should place a company scientist in the prize, and whether Mojsov's contested priority is a lesser risk than that.
Which second achievement, if any, should follow in a later year. B045 is my first choice, but Rosenberg's inclusion and Eshhar's omission remain unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented involvement with any credited name on the shortlisted candidates, and my research (single-cell genomics, brain atlases, spatial transcriptomics) does not overlap with B028, B045, B020 or B014. I note that Rickard Sandberg disclosed co-authorship with me, and none of it concerns a shortlisted candidate. Optogenetics is adjacent to neuroscience but I have no documented involvement with it.
